blocks.text: A hallucination is a hallucination of something that doesn't objectively exist. As small as a dream, as large as violent distortion; from nothing appearing on the left to reworked material on the right. Hallucination always produces something that wasn't there before, sometimes interesting, sometimes painful. The only thing we can be sure of inside a hallucination is 'I think, therefore I am'.
A hallucination doesn't exist objectively, but it exists subjectively.

Its material is taken from the unconscious: past memories, or imagination from within, worked under some motive into images and sounds. A hallucination always satisfies the wish of the motive that induced it — spontaneous psychological hallucinations satisfy unconscious wishes and resolve unconscious conflicts; drug-induced hallucinations may simply be unconscious content projected outward. So a hallucination isn't just 'seeing something that isn't there'; it's 'something stored inside you, projected onto the wall'.

First, separate illusion from hallucination. An illusion is a misreading of some perception: in dim light you take a wall shadow for a person, and when the light is restored the shadow disappears. A hallucination adds a perception out of nothing: restore the light and the shadow person is still there — that's a hallucination. Illusion doesn't add perception; hallucination does. An overconfident illusion is called a delusion.

By sense: auditory hallucination is the most common, usually human speech — everyday chatter mixed together, cursing, loving words, one sentence repeated over and over; some people stuff cotton in their ears, some curse back at the hallucination, some listen. Visual hallucination is the most representative: some paint and write on the walls, some black out their vision and bring out shadow people, some create characters hard to tell from real, some just get extra noise in the visual field. Olfactory hallucination smells strange fragrances, foul odours, blood, burning, perfume, the smell of a park, the smell of roast chicken. Gustatory hallucination tastes something odd and refuses food. Tactile hallucination feels insects crawling, electric current, fire, hands grabbing. In proprioceptive hallucination a still body feels some part moving, or loses balance and takes strange postures.

By whether external perception is needed: internal and external hallucination. Internal hallucination is equivalent to a dream — it arises with eyes closed; your favourite character sits on the bay window, and the bay window isn't the starting point, the character can sit on a chair or a table; reality's vision is simply treated as a dream, and then autonomous entities are added inside the dream. External hallucination needs perception to happen — with eyes open, on the walls, on the ceiling, at the edge of vision. Both can be explained by dream interpretation: a hallucination is a reflection of psychological content, a kind of imagination.

There is also phosphene: the perception of light when there is no light, chequers, honeycombs, spirals, starbursts, constant geometric shapes. Press your eyeball and you'll see them. And near-death experience: calm, separation from the body, passing through a tunnel, seeing a bright light, entering the light — out-of-body experience, life review, meeting the dead. And autonomous entities: 'people' that seem to have perception and autonomy, standing at the edge of vision; turn your head and they're gone, don't turn and they're always there.

Schizophrenia can be called a disease of hallucination. But hallucination itself doesn't equal illness: dream images are a kind of visual hallucination, and pressing your eyeball gives you phosphenes. The difference is whether it interferes with life, whether it's taken as real, and whether it brings pain.
At least reality isn't a hallucination; every hallucination is just my own rich imagination.
